blocks.md: Three phrases carry an astonishing amount of weight in Korea. Get these right and people will help you with the rest.

items.tip: Hello. Works morning, noon, night, stranger, boss, anyone.
Thank you. Note: 합니다 is said “ham-ni-da” — the ㅂ turns into ㅁ before ㄴ.
I am sorry. Also used for “excuse me” when squeezing past someone.

blocks.md: **안녕하세요 is a question in disguise.** It literally asks “are you at peace?”. That is why it works as both hello and how-are-you, and why nobody expects a real answer.

blocks.q: Someone holds a door for you. What do you say?
You need to get past someone on a crowded subway.
blocks.why: 죄송합니다 covers “sorry” and “excuse me”. 잠시만요 (jam-si-man-yo, “just a moment”) also works.

blocks.q: Say it. Warm and slightly rising at the end.

blocks.md: Korean sentences end with the verb, and the most useful verb is **“to be”**. In polite everyday speech it is 예요 / 이에요.

head: If the word ends in…
Use
Example
rows: 저는 학생**이에요** — I am a student

blocks.md: Why two forms? Purely for the mouth. 마크이에요 is a mouthful; 마크예요 is not. Korean does this a lot — the grammar bends so the sentence stays easy to say.
저 is “I” (humble). 는 marks it as the topic — “speaking of me…”. You will meet 는/은 everywhere.

blocks.q: Your name is Anna. Which is right?
blocks.why: 안나 ends in a vowel (ㅏ), so 예요.

blocks.q: You want to say “I am a student” (학생).
blocks.why: 학생 ends in ㅇ — a consonant — so 이에요.

blocks.q: Build “I am Korean.”  (한국 사람 = Korean person)

blocks.md: The single most useful question when you cannot read a menu.

items.tip: that thing over there (near neither of us)

blocks.md: **Korean splits “that” into two.** 그거 is close to the listener; 저거 is far from both. Point at a dish on your own table → 이거. Point across the restaurant → 저거.

blocks.q: You point at something on the far wall of the shop. Which word?

blocks.md: Point, ask, and the reply comes back in the same shape: **이거 김치예요** — “this is kimchi”.

blocks.q: Rising at the end, like any question.

blocks.md: Korean has **two** number systems. That sounds terrible and is actually fine, because they do different jobs and you can learn one at a time.

blocks.h: Sino-Korean — for money, dates, phone numbers
blocks.md: This is the one that matters first, because it is the one prices use.
**Big numbers just stack.** 십 (10) + 이 (2) = 십이 (12). 이 (2) + 십 (10) = 이십 (20). Twenty-three is 이십삼. No new words after ten.
**만 = 10,000.** Korean counts in units of ten thousand, not thousand. A 10,000-won note is 만 원. Coffee at 5,000 is 오천 원.

blocks.q: A price tag says 이만 원. Roughly how much?

blocks.md: Two phrases and a number, and you can shop anywhere in the country.

items.tip: Please give me — the workhorse of ordering.
This one, please. Point and say it.

blocks.md: **주세요 solves almost everything.** Put any noun in front of it and you have a polite request. 물 주세요 — water, please. 계산서 주세요 — the bill, please.

blocks.q: You are at a market stall and want to know the price.

blocks.md:
For small numbers of objects Korean uses the *other* number system with a counter word. You only need three: **하나, 둘, 셋** (1, 2, 3) → 하나 becomes **한**, 둘 becomes **두**, 셋 becomes **세** before a counter.

커피 **두 잔** 주세요 — two cups of coffee, please.
You will need this before you need almost anything else.
**Korean asks in one lump.** No “is”, no “the”, no word order gymnastics — noun, then question word, done. 역 어디예요? works exactly the same way.

blocks.q: Someone answers 저기예요. What did they say?

blocks.md: **여기요!** (yeo-gi-yo) — literally “here!”, used to call a server in a restaurant. Not rude at all; it is what everyone says.
Answering is where beginners freeze. These four get you through it.

items.tip: Yes. Also used as “uh-huh” to show you are listening.

blocks.h: The sentence that buys you patience
blocks.md:
**한국어 조금 해요** — “I speak a little Korean.”

Say this early in a conversation and people slow down for you. It works far better than apologising.
**네 is not only “yes”.** Koreans say it constantly during a conversation to mean “I am with you”. If someone 네-네-네s while you talk, they are not agreeing to anything — they are listening.

blocks.q: Someone asks you something you did not catch at all.
blocks.why: 몰라요 — “I do not know”. Honest and completely normal.

blocks.q: The most useful sentence in this course.

blocks.md: Nothing new. Everything below is something you already learned — put together the way it actually happens in a café.

blocks.q: 사천 원 — how much is that?

blocks.why: 아메리카노(americano) · 카페라떼(café latte) · 에스프레소(espresso) · 녹차(green tea)

blocks.meaning: How much is it? — It is 4,000 won.

blocks.why: 감사합니다(thank you) · 안녕하세요(hello) · 미안합니다(sorry) · 안녕히 가세요(goodbye)

blocks.md: That is a complete transaction, start to finish, in a language you could not read an hour ago.
